principles.evidence_reason: Membership is by shareholding and the service area is a well-defined roughly ten-square-mile footprint with 12,683 eAR connections. The SABL service-area boundary is present but Not Verified by the State, and the shareholder roll is not in the record, so the documentation is present but rests on a weaker source than a State-verified polygon.
principles.finding: Members are shareholders, and the service area covers roughly ten square miles with 12,683 eAR connections.
principles.signal: eAR total connections 12,683; about ten square miles served.

principles.name: Rules fit local conditions
principles.evidence_reason: A uniform volumetric rate documents that cost is tied to volume in principle, but metering is still being completed under the 2025 State mandate, so charges have historically been flat and do not yet track each member's actual use. Congruence is documented as a work in progress, so the evidence is partial.
principles.finding: A uniform volumetric rate ties cost to volume, but metering is still being completed under the 2025 State mandate, so charges were historically flat.
principles.signal: eAR rate structure: Uniform Usage; metering conversion underway.

principles.name: Collective-choice arrangements
principles.evidence_reason: The audited-statement notice documents a real, recurring mechanism: annual election of five directors, proxy voting, a 20 percent quorum, and a right to bring stockholder proposals. This is the best-documented collective-choice machinery among the three mutuals. Turnout and contested elections are not in the record.
principles.finding: Stockholders elect five directors each year, vote by proxy, and may bring stockholder proposals at the annual meeting.
principles.signal: Audited-statement notice: annual election of five directors, 20 percent quorum, proxy voting, stockholder proposals.

principles.name: Monitoring
principles.evidence_reason: The company publishes an annual audited financial statement (an independent financial monitor the other two mutuals lack) and the State rates it Not At-Risk with zero violations, so monitoring is independently documented on two fronts. The audit's scope and any operational-performance monitoring beyond the financial statements and the state risk screen are not in the record.
principles.finding: The company issues an annual audited financial statement and the State risk assessment shows it Not At-Risk with zero violations.
principles.signal: Annual audited income statement; SAFER Not At-Risk, 0 of 6 categories.

principles.name: Graduated sanctions
principles.evidence_reason: No schedule of graduated sanctions for non-payment or rule violations appears anywhere in the record. NOT DOCUMENTED means the supporting record was not found; it is a documentary gap, not a finding that the company fails to enforce its rules or governs badly.
principles.finding: A schedule of graduated sanctions for non-payment or rule violations is not in the record.
principles.signal: Not reported.

principles.name: Conflict-resolution mechanisms
principles.evidence_reason: Monthly open board meetings and legal counsel on retainer document a standing, regular local forum and access to counsel. The record documents a general governance venue rather than a dedicated dispute-resolution or member-grievance procedure with defined steps.
principles.finding: Monthly open board meetings and legal counsel on retainer provide a standing local forum.
principles.signal: Monthly open board meetings; legal firm on retainer.

principles.name: Recognized right to organize
principles.evidence_reason: Documented independently by the State Water Board as a privately owned mutual water company and by the IRS as a 501(c)(12). The record documents baseline legal recognition common to every lawful mutual, with no record of the right being actively used to reshape governance. The California Secretary of State holds the company as a registered corporation, entity number 0089591, first registered 10/30/1919, status as filed "Active", with a governing body named in the Statement of Information filed 6/10/2026. That is a direct state record of the right to organize being recognized, so the evidence behind this status is now a filed corporate record rather than an inference from the company's tax form. The status was already DOCUMENTED and does not move.
principles.finding: Recognized by the State Water Board as a privately owned mutual water company and by the IRS as a 501(c)(12).
principles.signal: eAR ownership 'Privately owned Mutual Water Company'; IRS 501(c)(12).

principles.name: Nested enterprises
principles.evidence_reason: The company purchases surface water and belongs to the Water Association of Kern County, so participation in the wider Kern water network is documented. No formal shared-governance body or agreement is documented, so the nesting on record is an informal membership and a purchase relationship rather than a governed layer, and the evidence is partial.
principles.finding: Purchases surface water and sits within the Kern County water network alongside neighboring districts, though a formal shared-governance body is not documented.
principles.signal: eAR purchased surface water; Water Association of Kern County member.

anomalies.title: FY2024 expense drop and net income swing
anomalies.flag_reason: Flagged because total spending dropped sharply in one year (down about 48 percent), driven mostly by a few large expense lines that were reported in earlier years but not the latest one. Nothing is adjusted; every figure is carried exactly as filed.

what.text: FY2024 total functional expenses (Form 990 Part IX line 25) fell to $5,702,750 from $11,023,709 in FY2023, a 48 percent drop, while total revenue (Part VIII line 12) held roughly flat ($11,267,619 vs $11,329,134), so net income (Part I, revenue less expenses) rose to $5,564,869 from $305,425. The drop is concentrated in 2 filer-itemized Other expenses lines (Part IX line 24) present in prior years but absent in FY2024: ANNUAL ENTITLEMENT ($2,098,365 FY2022, $2,314,598 FY2023) and CAPITAL FAC ($1,994,193 FY2022, $1,995,518 FY2023). structure.display: Uniform: fixed base plus a single volumetric rate, billed monthly, priced per HCF

cohort_position.title: Cohort position

components.name: Equity as a share of assets

cohort_position.what_this_is: Where this system sits among this project's own filers on each anchor metric, as a quartile of the whole mutual cohort. Each metric is placed on its own. The quartiles are never added up, weighted, ranked or turned into a single figure: this is a position, not a grade, not a rating, and not a ranking of companies. A metric this system does not report, or that is not comparable enough to place, is named above rather than counted against it.
cohort_position.cohort_note: The cohort is the mutual water companies in this project that file a Form 990 carrying financial data, which is not a sample of California's mutuals. Each metric places only the systems that report it at comparability tier A or B, so the n differs by metric and is stated on every line.

denominators.title: System Size and Water Use
denominators.note: System size and water use per fiscal year (the operating denominators that per-customer and per-acre metrics divide by), each cited to file and field. The eAR is reported on the calendar year; the 990 fiscal year differs by company. A calendar-year filer's volume is the eAR annual total (fiscal year = calendar year); an offset filer's is recast by a true monthly sum of the covered calendar months, or read not reported naming the missing months. Point-in-time counts (connections, population) are matched to the closest eAR year and never summed. Every derived figure states its formula and accounting rationale.
denominators.monthly_source: California open-data portal (data.ca.gov): the separate Produced Water (by month and source) and Delivered Water (by month and connection type) resources, which cover every public water system (not only urban suppliers), one resource per reporting year, matched by exact PWSID. This is the aggregate publication of eAR Section 6.

member.source: Form 990 Part III (DELIVERY OF WATER TO 11,500 MEMBERS)

member_vs_customer.difference_note: As found: 12,207 service connections and 11,500 members, a difference of 707. Stated as found and not reconciled.
member_vs_customer.sdwis_member_note: SDWIS reports 13,172 service connections while the member count is 11,500; a different basis (metered connections vs members). Both preserved, not reconciled.
member_vs_customer.explainer: In a mutual water company a MEMBER is a shareholder who owns part of the system; a CUSTOMER is a metered service connection that receives water. The two diverge because one owner can hold several connections, a connection can serve people who are not owners, and some mutuals attach shares to land by acreage rather than counting heads. Per-customer metrics divide by service connections; per-member metrics divide by shareholders; the two counts are never used interchangeably.

rollup.note: DERIVED, medium confidence, and shown beside the as-filed classes above, never in place of them. Every figure here is a sum of the filed class figures named on each cell; nothing is estimated and no filed value is altered. Two axes rather than four buckets because the filed classes are not mutually exclusive: the 2023-2024 form files residential non-potable deliveries, which belong to both. Commercial and institutional share one filed column and are not separable from the source, so the bucket keeps both words. The filed urban total is the potable total, so potable buckets reconcile against it and any difference is shown as a residual rather than absorbed; non-potable sits outside it by the survey's own design. A year in which a filed unit could not be recognized is marked incomplete, because the convertible subset is not the system's total. The filed urban total covers URBAN potable deliveries only: agricultural irrigation sits outside it, as does every non-potable class, by the survey's own design and not because anything is missing. Both are reported separately beside it.

how_built.title: How this was built
how_built.intro: A plain account of the forensic lineage behind the hard-to-source metrics: what sources were checked, what was found, what was derived, and what could not be built and why. Every figure marked DERIVED or IMPOSSIBLE above is traceable to a line here.

sources_checked: State Water Board eAR Section 8b (water-rate revenue B1.1/B1.2)
State Water Board eAR Section 4 (connection count, same reporting year)
audited financial statement (secondary cross-check, where published)
entries.found: The eAR Section 8b reports water-rate revenue for reporting year 2023, so this is a DIRECT filed figure; per customer it is divided by the eAR Section 4 connection count for the same reporting year, so numerator and denominator share the year.
entries.note: No like-for-like cross-check available: the only staged audited statement covers the June 30, 2024 fiscal year, a DIFFERENT fiscal year than the eAR Section 8b period (the fiscal year ending June 30, 2023). Cross-checks compare like fiscal years only, so the audit's Water Sales and Related Charges of $9,348,617 (page 2) is not compared against the eAR figure here.

sources_checked: State Water Board eAR Section 8b (water-rate revenue B1.1/B1.2)
entries.found: No source separately reports a member assessment, so it is DERIVED as a residual: $10,868,355 (990 program-service revenue) minus $8,042,213 (eAR water-rate revenue) = $2,826,142. Period-aligned; medium confidence.
entries.note: For Oildale this residual is NOT cleanly assessment revenue: it partly reflects the unreconciled gap between the eAR Section 8b total and the Form 990 total for the same fiscal year, so part of it is a source-to-source difference rather than a distinct assessment line.

State Water Board eAR Section 8b (revenue lines)
entries.found: The rate price exists in Section 8a but no revenue or tier volume is reported, and the base charge is already inside water sales.
entries.note: The eAR Section 8a reports a base/meter rate PRICE, but the filing carries no meter revenue line and no tier volume, and the base charge is already inside the water-sales revenue (eAR Section 8b water rates). Building a separate meter figure would double-count. Not backed into from a total.

blocks.title: Who they are
blocks.body: A mutual water company serving Oildale, a working-class unincorporated community directly north of Bakersfield in Kern County, at the south end of the San Joaquin Valley. Every retail customer is a shareholder. [3] By connection count, among the largest mutuals in California, an order of magnitude above the typical mutual.

blocks.title: How the money works
blocks.body: Metered retail sales to shareholder-customers with rates published on the company site. [1] Dominant cost driver is purchased treated water through North of the River Municipal Water District (NORMWD) and Kern County Water Agency Improvement District 4. [2][4] Since 2009, dual plumbing in new business parks substitutes untreated groundwater for landscape and fire lines, cutting treated water costs. [1]

blocks.title: Where the water comes from
blocks.body: Purchased treated State Water Project water is primary; local groundwater has been emergency-only since state deliveries began in 1977. [1] The 2005 regional agreement doubled the Henry C. Garnett purification plant, securing long-term treated supply. [4] Supply read: single dominant wholesale source with an emergency groundwater buffer; supply security rests on contracts rather than owned sources.

blocks.title: Infrastructure and its age
blocks.body: Distribution system originating 1919, extended across a century of growth; current four-acre headquarters and operations base built 1999; system-wide remote meter reading installed 2009; absorbed more than 1,800 NORMWD retail connections and associated facilities in 2014. [1][4] Accounting read: reinvestment above depreciation on the dashboard window. [D]

A falling trend means reinvestment is renewing the plant faster than it wears down. This shares its inputs with the Asset Consumption Ratio on the tearsheet.

blocks.title: How they got here
blocks.body: Founded 1919 by Oildale residents during the oil boom. [1] Helped form NORMWD in 1969 as a public wholesale agency to import State Water Project supply. [4] In 2014 an integration agreement made NORMWD wholesale-only and moved its retail customers to Oildale. [1][4]

blocks.title: Who runs it and how
blocks.body: Elected five-member board serving one-year terms; Jude Hupp president, Ryan Nunneley general manager; professional staff with named engineering, legal, and audit firms on retainer. [1][2] Style read: the most institutionally transparent mutual in the cohort: monthly open board meetings, bylaws, agendas, and audited financial statements posted publicly. [1] One-year board terms keep directors continuously accountable to shareholders. Rate posture: published schedule; revenue tracking expense growth on the dashboard. [D]

blocks.title: On the record
blocks.body: 1982: Highland Park Public Utility District, the other original Oildale retailer, merged into NORMWD. [4] 2014: NORMWD retail integration. [1][4] No litigation surfaced in public search results; recorded as not found, not as a clean bill.

compliance.plain_sentence: The State Water Board's SAFER assessment lists this system as Not At-Risk. Retrieved from the state's published file on 2026-08-27.
compliance.source: California State Water Resources Control Board, Division of Drinking Water: SAFER Drinking Water Risk Assessment Public Flat File, data.ca.gov resource 255887bb-5451-4c19-8e35-27899ae8c3ad

blocks.title: Strengths
blocks.body: Scale: 13,000 connections spread fixed costs an order of magnitude wider than the typical mutual [2][D]. Transparency posture (published audits, open meetings, posted rates) that exceeds AB 240 minimums [1]. Professional management with institutional depth: named GM, retained engineers, auditor, counsel [2]. Demonstrated structural adaptability: formed a wholesale district in 1969, absorbed its retail arm in 2014 [4]. Cost engineering culture: dual plumbing and remote metering adopted early [1].

blocks.title: Weak points and watch items
blocks.body: Single dominant supply source held by contract, not ownership; wholesale price escalation passes straight to members [1][4]. Service area demographics imply affordability limits on rate flexibility; Kern County is the state's most violation-heavy county in the UCLA research, a hard operating environment. Emergency-only groundwater means drought resilience depends on State Water Project reliability, which is declining statewide. Flat valley urban setting carries minimal WUI risk, but San Joaquin subsidence and SGMA groundwater politics are long-run watch items.

narrative.supply_profile: Oildale serves the Bakersfield area and relies on Kern River and purchased surface water plus groundwater, with system metering still being completed, so its supply and cost move with Central Valley hydrology.
narrative.cost_link: For Oildale the weather link runs mainly through cost, not revenue: dry years shift it from surface water to pumped groundwater, raising energy and treatment expense, while its historically flat billing kept revenue steadier than a metered peer's.

dimensions.label: Water-year type
dimensions.read: A dry water-year type cuts Kern River and project surface-water deliveries, pushing Oildale toward more groundwater pumping, which raises energy and treatment cost.

dimensions.label: Drought stage
dimensions.read: Kern County drought stage drives conservation, but because much of Oildale's billing was historically flat rather than metered, dry-year demand changes hit its revenue less directly than a fully metered system.

dimensions.label: Precipitation
dimensions.read: Local and statewide precipitation feed the Kern River and the valley aquifer Oildale draws on, so a dry precipitation year is a lower-surface-supply, higher-pumping-cost year for it.

dimensions.label: Snowpack
dimensions.read: Southern Sierra snowpack feeds the Kern River, a core Oildale supply, so a thin snowpack year directly reduces its cheapest surface water and raises reliance on pumped groundwater.

dimensions.label: State Water Project allocation
dimensions.read: State Water Project allocation matters to Oildale through Kern County Water Agency deliveries; a low allocation year tightens the regional surface-water pool it buys into.

weather_exposure.title: Weather exposure
weather_exposure.lead: A computed read, not a self-report. Three separately sourced components: how much of the service area sits in mapped fire hazard, how much of this company's own filing window its county spent in severe drought, and how exposed its water supply is to a dry year. Each carries its own source and check date, and a component that cannot be computed says so rather than going blank.

composite.basis: Composed from 3 of 3 components (Fire hazard, Drought regime, Supply sensitivity).

components.name: Fire hazard
components.value: About 4.5% of the service area sits in the High or Very High fire hazard zones California maps, and the most severe class mapped there is High.

The share is integrated over 600 scan rows of about 12.19 m, so it is approximate to that resolution and is not an exact acreage.
components.source: CAL FIRE Fire Hazard Severity Zones (fhsz24_1), State and Local Responsibility Areas, intersected with the State Water Board SABL service-area boundary
components.logic: The service-area boundary the State Water Board publishes is laid over the fire hazard severity zones CAL FIRE publishes, and the share of the service area inside each class is measured. High and Very High are reported together because those are the classes California attaches building and defensible-space requirements to.

components.value: Across the years this company filed (2020-07-01 to 2024-06-30), Kern County was in severe drought or worse 55.8% of the time.

It ties the water conditions to the years the financial statements were actually lived through, rather than to a fixed recent period.

components.confidence_reason: Each of the facts underneath is a published record carried at high confidence, except a residual share, which is a subtraction and is carried at medium and labelled. Combining them into a sensitivity band is a derivation, which BLUEPRINT 5 puts at medium.
components.band_basis_note: The dependence is taken from this system's own 2024 Consumer Confidence Report, which states a quantified mix.

components.logic: Three things decide how hard a dry year lands on a system's supply: what it draws on, whether it controls a second source of its own, and whether the ground under it is already being pumped beyond what the state considers sustainable. Buying treated water from a wholesaler is the most exposed position, because the decision to cut back in a dry year is not the system's to make. What a system draws on is read from its own annual report where that report states a mix, and from the State Water Board inventory otherwise.

governance.title: Institutional design: Ostrom's eight principles (evidence status)

overall.summary: 6 documented, 2 partial, 0 not documented of eight principles.
overall.reason: A count of how many of Elinor Ostrom's eight design principles have a supporting record on file, not a grade. NOT DOCUMENTED means the supporting record was not found, not that the company governs badly. It marks a gap in the documentary record, an evidence gap to close, never a governance failing.

governance.not_documented_distinction: NOT DOCUMENTED means the supporting record was not found, not that the company governs badly. It marks a gap in the documentary record, an evidence gap to close, never a governance failing.
governance.note: Each mutual is read against Elinor Ostrom's eight design principles for institutions that govern a shared resource durably. Per principle: a one-line finding, the observable signal, a citation, and an evidence status stating whether the supporting record exists: DOCUMENTED (a cited record supports alignment), PARTIAL (some evidence exists but it is incomplete), or NOT DOCUMENTED (no supporting record was found). This is an evidence-status read, not a grade: the principles are never ranked, weighted, or given a letter, consistent with reporting as filed and not grading companies. NOT DOCUMENTED means the supporting record was not found, not that the company governs badly. It marks a gap in the documentary record, an evidence gap to close, never a governance failing.

principles.name: Clearly defined boundaries
principles.evidence_reason: The membership is sharply defined (230 named shareholders) and the service area is the East End of the Ojai Valley with 249 connections over about 3.5 square miles, so the record documents who is in and who is out. The SABL boundary is present but Not Verified by the State, so the outer edge rests on a weaker source than a verified polygon.
principles.finding: Members are 230 shareholders, and the service area is the East End of the Ojai Valley with 249 eAR connections.
principles.signal: eAR total connections 249; 230 shareholders; about 3.5 square miles.

principles.name: Rules fit local conditions
principles.evidence_reason: A published rate schedule and Rules and Regulations document the terms of service and charges. Billing is share-based (charges scale with shares held, not metered consumption), so the record documents cost tracking ownership rather than actual use, a weaker form of proportionality.
principles.finding: A published rate schedule and Rules and Regulations tie charges to service and set the terms of use.
principles.signal: Corporate documents: Water Rates and Charges, Rules and Regulations.

principles.name: Collective-choice arrangements
principles.evidence_reason: The strongest collective-choice evidence in the cohort is concrete: shareholders voted to approve a 500,000 dollar tank loan in 2020 and voted down a proposed sale of the company around 2005, so the record documents members deciding major capital questions. The evidence is two recalled votes rather than a documented record of elections, turnout, and routine decisions.
principles.finding: Shareholders vote on major capital: they approved a 500,000 dollar tank loan in 2020 and refused a sale around 2005.
principles.signal: Shareholder votes on capital and on a proposed sale (context page).

principles.name: Monitoring
principles.evidence_reason: Connections are metered, water-quality monitoring is in place, and the State rates the system Not At-Risk, so operational monitoring is documented. No independent audited financial statement is published, so the financial side of monitoring rests on the system's own unaudited numbers, leaving the evidence partial.
principles.finding: Metering and water-quality monitoring are in place and the State shows the system Not At-Risk, but no independent audited financial statement is published.
principles.signal: eAR metered connections; SAFER Not At-Risk; audited financials not published.

principles.name: Graduated sanctions
principles.evidence_reason: Corporate documents include a written Water Shut-Off Policy, a Leak Policy, and Rules and Regulations, so consequences for non-payment and misuse are documented and published. The record documents that sanctions exist but not that they are graduated into escalating steps scaling with severity or repetition.
principles.finding: Corporate documents include a written Water Shut-Off Policy, a Leak Policy, and Rules and Regulations.
principles.signal: Corporate documents: Shut-Off Policy, Leak Policy, Rules and Regulations.

principles.name: Conflict-resolution mechanisms
principles.evidence_reason: This is the best-documented conflict path of the three: published Rules and Regulations and Administrative Policies, board minutes on the public record, and a named General Counsel document a real, traceable route to raise and resolve disputes. A dedicated member-grievance or appeals procedure with defined steps is not documented.
principles.finding: Published Rules and Regulations, Administrative Policies, board minutes, and named general counsel provide a local resolution path.
principles.signal: Corporate documents and a General Counsel page; published board minutes.

principles.name: Recognized right to organize
principles.evidence_reason: The right is well documented: Articles of Incorporation are on file and both the State Water Board and the IRS recognize the mutual (a 501(c)(12)). As with the other mutuals, the record documents baseline legal standing rather than a documented instance of the right being exercised to change how the system is run. The California Secretary of State holds the company as a registered corporation, entity number 0133485, first registered 04/11/1929, status as filed "Active", with a governing body named in the Statement of Information filed 6/2/2026. That is a direct state record of the right to organize being recognized, so the evidence behind this status is now a filed corporate record rather than an inference from the company's tax form. The status was already DOCUMENTED and does not move.
principles.finding: Incorporated as a mutual water company (Articles of Incorporation on file) and recognized by the State Water Board and the IRS as a 501(c)(12).
principles.signal: Articles of Incorporation; eAR ownership; IRS 501(c)(12).

principles.name: Nested enterprises
principles.evidence_reason: The system draws on the shared Ojai groundwater basin and has run FEMA-funded post-Thomas-Fire recovery projects, so embedding in larger physical and disaster-response systems is documented. Its role in basin governance is not documented, so the nesting on record is physical and project-based rather than an ongoing governed layer, leaving the evidence partial.
principles.finding: Draws on the shared Ojai groundwater basin and has run FEMA-funded post-fire recovery projects, though its role in basin governance is not documented in the record.
principles.signal: Ojai Valley groundwater reliance; FEMA post-Thomas-Fire projects.

denominators.note: System size and water use per fiscal year (the operating denominators that per-customer and per-acre metrics divide by), each cited to file and field. The eAR is reported on the calendar year; the 990 fiscal year differs by company. A calendar-year filer's volume is the eAR annual total (fiscal year = calendar year); an offset filer's is recast by a true monthly sum of the covered calendar months, or read not reported naming the missing months. member_vs_customer.sdwis_member_note: SDWIS reports 249 service connections while the member count is 230; a different basis (metered connections vs members). Both preserved, not reconciled.
member_vs_customer.explainer: In a mutual water company a MEMBER is a shareholder who owns part of the system; a CUSTOMER is a metered service connection that receives water. The two diverge because one owner can hold several connections, a connection can serve people who are not owners, and some mutuals attach shares to land by acreage rather than counting heads. Per-customer metrics divide by service connections; per-member metrics divide by shareholders; the two counts are never used interchangeably.

calendar_basis.short: Calendar year, not the fiscal year ending March 31
calendar_basis.label: Different reporting periods. The DWR PWSS survey year is a calendar year ending December 31; this system's fiscal year ends March 31. A fiscal year therefore shares three of its twelve months with the calendar year it is named for and the other nine with the calendar year before it. Read the two side by side with that in mind. Neither series is recast: both are reported as filed. The survey year runs January to December, with the filed annual total reported as filed and never computed from the twelve months.

rollup.title: Derived comparability view (customer type by water quality)
rollup.note: DERIVED, medium confidence, and shown beside the as-filed classes above, never in place of them. Every figure here is a sum of the filed class figures named on each cell; nothing is estimated and no filed value is altered. Two axes rather than four buckets because the filed classes are not mutually exclusive: the 2023-2024 form files residential non-potable deliveries, which belong to both. Commercial and institutional share one filed column and are not separable from the source, so the bucket keeps both words. The filed urban total is the potable total, so potable buckets reconcile against it and any difference is shown as a residual rather than absorbed; non-potable sits outside it by the survey's own design. A year in which a filed unit could not be recognized is marked incomplete, because the convertible subset is not the system's total. The filed urban total covers URBAN potable deliveries only: agricultural irrigation sits outside it, as does every non-potable class, by the survey's own design and not because anything is missing. Both are reported separately beside it.

coverage.filed: 12 survey years, 2013 to 2024. Production carries a positive figure in all 12 of those years, across 4 sources. Deliveries carry a positive figure in 11 of the 12 years, across 9 customer classes.
coverage.tail: Separately, 58 cells were filed as zero, which is a figure the system reported and not an absence, and 24 were left blank. 8 figures carry a unit the survey's code list does not contain; those are shown as filed and were not converted, because a guessed unit would be a guessed volume.

pwss_volume.note: Annual water volume as filed with the California Department of Water Resources Public Water System Statistics survey, 2013 to 2024. Each system chooses its own unit of measure and the choice is not stable from year to year, so the acre-feet column is a DERIVED normalization at medium confidence and the filed value and its unit, shown on hover and in the logic panel, are the source of truth at high confidence. Years this system did not file are absent rather than zero. For 2013 and later the State Water Board (eAR and SAFER) is the standard and this DWR series is a backup, except the 2023-2024 SAFER years, which are Water Boards data. Nothing here is reconciled against another source.

sgma_basin.title: Groundwater basin (DWR, SGMA)

basins.name: OJAI VALLEY
basins.plain_lead: The Department of Water Resources ranks this basin High priority, its top tier, and has not designated it in critical overdraft, so the state has not found the basin is being pumped faster than it naturally refills. A Groundwater Sustainability Agency is the local body SGMA makes responsible for bringing a basin into balance. One agency is named for this basin, listed below.
basins.gsa_text: Ojai Basin Groundwater Management Agency GSA
basins.gw_level_comment:
1) There are many wells that are showing large declines from the late 90's and many more that show significant declines since 2010/11. Only a few show some bump to the higher precipitation year 2017. 

No indications of full recoverys from dry periods as expected from past precipitation responses (see note 2).

Sources 4-002_7a_Hydrographs.docx   DWR Data Viewer - Examples  - 344475N1192412W001  (-53.72),  344606N1192312W001 (-132.30 ft) 344539N1192309W001 (-84.5) 344550N1192406W001 (-162 ft before 62ft bump from higher precipitation) 

2) In the Ojai Valley, the water level elevation in key Well No. 04N22W05L08S was down 50.2 feet from the 2013 measurement after having been down 78.4 feet from the 2012 measurement. The Ojai Valley basin responds quickly to rainfall or the lack of rainfall, and it is not uncommon to see large drops in water level during dry periods and recovery to at or above normal levels during wet periods (see Hydrograph in Appendix B).
Source: 4-002_7a_VenturaCo2014AnnualReport.pdf pg. 73
basins.subsidence_comment: No documented groundwater extraction induced inelastic Subsidence
basins.join_note: SABL boundary verification: Not Verified (SABL). The areal join is derived and never better than the boundary it rests on.

sgma_basin.note: Basin priority, critical overdraft designation and the governing agency are published by the Department of Water Resources and are carried exactly as published (high confidence). Placing this system in a basin is an AREAL join: its service-area boundary is overlapped with the basin boundary, so the placement is derived and is never better than the boundary it rests on. That is why the join confidence reads medium or low and never high. Where a service area spans more than one basin every basin is listed and none is ranked, because the source does not say how much of the area lies in each. The groundwater-level line is DWR's own written finding for the basin, quoted rather than scored; no well record is read.

how_built.title: How this was built
how_built.intro: A plain account of the forensic lineage behind the hard-to-source metrics: what sources were checked, what was found, what was derived, and what could not be built and why. Every figure marked DERIVED or IMPOSSIBLE above is traceable to a line here.

sources_checked: State Water Board eAR Section 8b (water-rate revenue B1.1/B1.2)
State Water Board eAR Section 4 (connection count, same reporting year)
audited financial statement (secondary cross-check, where published)
entries.found: The eAR Section 8b reports water-rate revenue for reporting year 2023, so this is a DIRECT filed figure; per customer it is divided by the eAR Section 4 connection count for the same reporting year, so numerator and denominator share the year.

sources_checked: State Water Board eAR Section 8b (water-rate revenue B1.1/B1.2)
entries.found: A period-aligned residual cannot be computed for this filer, so the metric is rendered IMPOSSIBLE rather than guessed.
entries.note: Not derivable. The eAR Section 8b is the calendar year 2023 while the Form 990 fiscal year ends March 31, 2023; the two period ends are 9 months apart, so a period-aligned residual cannot be computed. And billing is share-based: monthly charges scale with the number of shares an owner holds, so the eAR water-rate line already IS the assessment - there is no separate assessment to residual out.

blocks.title: Who they are
blocks.body: A small mutual delivering both treated domestic water and untreated agricultural water to homes, citrus, and avocado ranches on steep canyon terrain. This is the size class the research literature flags as highest-risk, and its history shows both the failure pattern and the recovery pattern.

blocks.title: How the money works
blocks.body: Water charges and assessments to shareholders. The dominant historical cost was purchased water: in hot months the company once bought up to 80 percent of supply from Casitas Municipal Water District, and the 2015 strategy was explicitly to rebuild company sources to cut that bill. [1] Rates: not reported publicly in detail.

blocks.title: Where the water comes from
blocks.body: Three potable surface sources including the Senior Canyon tunnel and springs, five agricultural wells, an 80 acre-foot reservoir, and two Casitas interties for backup. [1] Gravity feeds the domestic system from the Thacher Tank. Supply read: locally sourced and gravity-cheap when the canyon produces, purchase-dependent when it does not; the tunnel is the swing asset.

blocks.title: Infrastructure and its age
blocks.body: A museum of eras: 1929 to 1930s tunnel and original steel mains, a reservoir expanded in the early 1960s from 1940s agricultural ponds, a late-1960s Thacher Tank replaced in 2020 with a 708,000 gallon tank, and 2023 to 2025 FEMA-rebuilt diversions, pipelines, and roads. [1][3] By the early 2000s the original assets had aged into failure: rusted scaled mains, a tunnel cave-in at 2,400 feet, a tank patched with epoxy annually. [1] Accounting read: the current reinvestment trend reflects the rebuild era. [D]

net_plant_age.logic: Accumulated depreciation as a share of gross plant (Form 990 Part X line 10b over line 10a): the portion of the system's plant already depreciated, a proxy for average plant age. A falling trend means reinvestment is renewing the plant faster than it wears down. This shares its inputs with the Asset Consumption Ratio on the tearsheet.

blocks.title: How they got here
blocks.body: Water rights trace to 1883 (Judge Hines dams the creek); a 1903 Ventura County judgment, after three trips to the California Supreme Court, adjudicated all flows of San Antonio Creek. [1] Five East End landowners incorporated the company in 1929 to water citrus and avocado land, then drilled the Senior Canyon tunnel, sited by Stanford geologist Bailey Willis. [1] Casitas arrived in the mid-1960s with an intertie. Decades of under-maintenance followed; around 2005 the board explored selling to Casitas, which wanted an estimated 5 million dollars of repairs first, and shareholders refused. [1] From 2015 the board chose revitalization: new tank (2020, 500,000 dollar shareholder-approved loan), remote monitoring, and tunnel renovation funded by a 2.65 million dollar state grant. [1]

blocks.title: Who runs it and how
blocks.body: Seven-member volunteer board plus a provisional management committee; four-person staff. [1] Style read: a volunteer-governed system that turned itself around, now publishing board minutes, shareholder meeting records, and corporate documents on its website; grant-seeking capability (state grant, FEMA awards) unusual for its size. Rate posture: shareholder-approved special funding (the 2020 loan) shows the membership will pay for capital when asked, the opposite of the rate-averse pathology. [1]

blocks.title: On the record
blocks.body: 1903: San Antonio Creek adjudication. [1] 2005: failed sale exploration to Casitas. [1] 2017: Thomas Fire surrounded and evacuated the Ojai Valley, establishing the terrain's fire exposure. [2] January 2023: atmospheric river floods destroyed surface diversions, pipelines, and access roads; federal disaster declaration; FEMA organized repairs into 10 projects, estimated 2.9 million dollars at 75 percent federal share, completion expected summer 2025; West Fork diversion dam rebuilt with a removable center section for future debris flows. [3]

blocks.title: Strengths
blocks.body: Adjudicated 1903 water rights and owned local sources: cheap gravity water when the canyon flows [1]. Demonstrated turnaround governance: shareholders funded a tank by loan, board won a 2.65 million dollar state grant and 2.9 million dollars of FEMA projects [1][3]. Post-disaster rebuild is producing newer-than-peer infrastructure at the critical points [1][3]. Membership that votes to invest rather than defer, the reverse of the classic small-mutual pathology [1].

blocks.title: Weak points and watch items
blocks.body: Textbook WUI exposure: fire above, debris flow below, and it has now taken the flood half of that punch [2][3]. 249 connections is deep inside the sub-500 danger zone; every fixed cost lands on a tiny base. Purchase dependency returns whenever canyon sources fall short; drought is a direct margin squeeze [1]. Volunteer governance is currently strong but thin by construction; continuity depends on a handful of people. FEMA's 75 percent share leaves a 25 percent local match on 2.9 million dollars of repairs, meaningful at this scale [3].

narrative.supply_profile: Senior Canyon draws on the local Ojai Valley groundwater basin with a Casitas Municipal Water District standby connection, so its supply is LOCAL: Ventura County rain and Lake Casitas storage, not the State Water Project.
narrative.cost_link: Senior Canyon's weather exposure is local and supply-side: a dry Ojai year lowers basin levels and leans it on the Casitas standby connection, raising cost. Because billing is share-based rather than metered volumetric, dry-year demand swings move its revenue less than its cost.

dimensions.label: Water-year type
dimensions.read: The Sacramento Valley water-year type shown here is a poor proxy for Senior Canyon: it is not on the State Water Project, so its supply follows local Ventura County conditions, which can diverge from the statewide type.

dimensions.label: Drought stage
dimensions.read: Local Ventura County drought stage is the dimension that matters most: a deep local drought lowers Ojai basin recharge and Lake Casitas storage, the two things Senior Canyon actually depends on.

dimensions.label: Precipitation
dimensions.read: Local precipitation, not the statewide 8-Station Index, recharges the Ojai basin Senior Canyon pumps from, so the statewide precipitation figure here understates or overstates its real supply picture in any given year.

dimensions.label: Snowpack
dimensions.read: Sierra snowpack is essentially irrelevant to Senior Canyon: its water comes from a coastal groundwater basin fed by local rain, not from Sierra melt or the State Water Project, so this row is context for the cohort, not a driver for this system.

dimensions.label: State Water Project allocation
dimensions.read: The State Water Project allocation does not reach Senior Canyon; it is shown for cohort comparison only. Its supply risk is local basin level and Casitas storage.

weather_exposure.title: Weather exposure
weather_exposure.lead: A computed read, not a self-report. Three separately sourced components: how much of the service area sits in mapped fire hazard, how much of this company's own filing window its county spent in severe drought, and how exposed its water supply is to a dry year. Each carries its own source and check date, and a component that cannot be computed says so rather than going blank.

composite.basis: Composed from 3 of 3 components (Fire hazard, Drought regime, Supply sensitivity).

components.value: About 45.1% of the service area sits in the High or Very High fire hazard zones California maps, and the most severe class mapped there is Very High.

High and Very High are reported together because those are the classes California attaches building and defensible-space requirements to.

components.confidence_reason: Each of the facts underneath is a published record carried at high confidence, except a residual share, which is a subtraction and is carried at medium and labelled. Combining them into a sensitivity band is a derivation, which BLUEPRINT 5 puts at medium.
components.band_basis_note: The dependence is taken from the State Water Board inventory's structured source type, which is the default wherever no report states a quantified mix.
components.cross_source_note: This system's own 2023 Consumer Confidence Report was located and read, and it describes its sources without stating a share or a volume for any of them, so there is no mix to read from it. The band above rests on the inventory's single source type. Ranking a supply out of the report's wording would be reading a category out of prose, which this component refuses to do.
components.cross_source_heading: This system's own report states no mix, and that was checked
components.source: State Water Board public water system inventory (data.ca.gov, Drinking Water Public Water System Information), primary water source type as published, matched by exact PWSID; eWRIMS water rights; DWR SGMA; https://ear.waterboards.ca.gov/Home/ViewCCR?PwsID=CA5601117&Year=2023
components.logic: Three things decide how hard a dry year lands on a system's supply: what it draws on, whether it controls a second source of its own, and whether the ground under it is already being pumped beyond what the state considers sustainable. Buying treated water from a wholesaler is the most exposed position, because the decision to cut back in a dry year is not the system's to make. What a system draws on is read from its own annual report where that report states a mix, and from the State Water Board inventory otherwise.

blocks.title: Who they are
blocks.body: An agricultural irrigation mutual water company (501(c)(12)) serving about 6,800 acres of farmland in the Somis area of the Las Posas Valley, southern Ventura County, on rolling agricultural valley terrain. [1] It delivers groundwater for irrigation only, explicitly not intended for domestic use (domestic service in the area is Ventura County Waterworks District No. 19), so it is not a State-regulated public drinking-water system and has no PWSID. [1][C]

blocks.title: How the money works
blocks.body: Revenue of about $2,772,912 in FY2025, from water charges and assessments to member-shareholders. [D] A detailed rate history beyond the filed schedule is not reported.

blocks.title: Where the water comes from
blocks.body: Supply is exclusively groundwater from the Las Posas Valley basin, delivered through 10 wells, a one-million-gallon reservoir, 25 miles of pipe, and three booster stations, about 5,000 acre-feet a year. [1]

blocks.title: Infrastructure and its age
blocks.body: Plant is read from the Form 990 balance sheet; the computed net plant age (accumulated depreciation as a share of gross plant) is shown with its multi-year trend. [990][D] Detailed infrastructure history is not reported in a public source.

source_lines: Form 990 Part X line 10a (land, buildings, and equipment; gross)
Form 990 Part X line 10b (accumulated depreciation)
net_plant_age.logic: Accumulated depreciation as a share of gross plant (Form 990 Part X line 10b over line 10a): the portion of the system's plant already depreciated, a proxy for average plant age. A falling trend means reinvestment is renewing the plant faster than it wears down. This shares its inputs with the Asset Consumption Ratio on the tearsheet.
net_plant_age.confidence_reason: A ratio derived from two filed Part X figures; medium per the BLUEPRINT confidence tiers (a derivation, not a direct line item).
net_plant_age.what_would_change: nothing; the value is comparable as filed

blocks.title: How they got here
blocks.body: The company grew out of Las Posas Water Company shareholders who wanted an agricultural delivery system: test wells were drilled in 1919 and two elevation-zone mutual companies formed in 1922 (about 2,800 and 1,200 acres), merging into the present company in 1947. IRS tax recognition dates to 1934 (a predecessor entity). [1][990]

blocks.title: Who runs it and how
blocks.body: Run by a contract General Manager (Bryan Bondy), a Water Superintendent, a Project Manager, and an Administrator, under a shareholder board; the company publishes an operations and adjudication record on its website. [1] Individual director names are not published.

blocks.title: On the record
blocks.body: Zone Mutual was a named defendant in the Las Posas Valley Groundwater Basin comprehensive adjudication (Fox Canyon Groundwater Management Agency), participating to preserve its pumping rights; final judgment was entered July 10, 2023 and affirmed on appeal. [2] No fire or flood impact to the system was found in the public record.

blocks.title: Strengths
blocks.body: An unusually well-documented agricultural mutual: it publishes its infrastructure, supply, and adjudication record, rare at this scale. [1] A large owned groundwater delivery system (10 wells, 25 miles of pipe, 5,000 acre-feet a year) on a single basin. [1] Its pumping right is now defined and protected by the 2023 Las Posas adjudication judgment. [2]

blocks.title: Weak points and watch items
blocks.body: A single-basin groundwater supplier now operating under an adjudication watermaster, so its pumping is capped and subject to basin management. [2] As an irrigation-only mutual its fortunes track agricultural land use and basin health; drought and pumping limits are direct risks. No financial statement beyond the Form 990 is public. [990]

weather_exposure.title: Weather exposure
weather_exposure.lead: A computed read, not a self-report. Three separately sourced components: how much of the service area sits in mapped fire hazard, how much of this company's own filing window its county spent in severe drought, and how exposed its water supply is to a dry year. Each carries its own source and check date, and a component that cannot be computed says so rather than going blank.

composite.absence: No composite is composed for this system. 1 of 3 components could be computed (Drought regime), which is not enough to compose a read over. The components that could not be computed are listed with the reason each one failed; a single reading presented as a composite would claim a completeness this system does not have.

components.name: Fire hazard
components.plain_lead: No service-area boundary is on file for this system, so there is no shape to lay over the fire hazard map. That is a missing outline, not a finding that the system faces no fire risk.
components.reason: No PWSID is recorded for this system, so there is no SABL service-area polygon to intersect with the hazard zone layer. The join is areal and there is no geometry to join with; this is a missing key, not a finding that the system faces no fire hazard.
components.source: CAL FIRE Fire Hazard Severity Zones (fhsz24_1), State and Local Responsibility Areas, intersected with the State Water Board SABL service-area boundary
components.value: not reported

components.name: Drought regime
components.value: Across the years this company filed (2020-01-01 to 2025-12-31), Ventura County was in severe drought or worse 42.8% of the time.

It ties the water conditions to the years the financial statements were actually lived through, rather than to a fixed recent period.

governance.title: Institutional design: Ostrom's eight principles (evidence status)

overall.summary: 6 documented, 0 partial, 2 not documented of eight principles.
overall.reason: A count of how many of Elinor Ostrom's eight design principles have a supporting record on file, not a grade. NOT DOCUMENTED means the supporting record was not found, not that the company governs badly. It marks a gap in the documentary record, an evidence gap to close, never a governance failing.

governance.not_documented_distinction: NOT DOCUMENTED means the supporting record was not found, not that the company governs badly. It marks a gap in the documentary record, an evidence gap to close, never a governance failing.
governance.note: Each mutual is read against Elinor Ostrom's eight design principles for institutions that govern a shared resource durably. Per principle: a one-line finding, the observable signal, a citation, and an evidence status stating whether the supporting record exists: DOCUMENTED (a cited record supports alignment), PARTIAL (some evidence exists but it is incomplete), or NOT DOCUMENTED (no supporting record was found). This is an evidence-status read, not a grade: the principles are never ranked, weighted, or given a letter, consistent with reporting as filed and not grading companies. NOT DOCUMENTED means the supporting record was not found, not that the company governs badly. It marks a gap in the documentary record, an evidence gap to close, never a governance failing.

principles.name: Clearly defined boundaries
principles.evidence_reason: SDWIS defines the membership as a fixed set of service connections and the State Water Board publishes a SABL service-area polygon, so who is inside and outside the system is documented. The boundary is Verified, so its outer edge rests on that State layer.
principles.finding: The system is a defined public water system: 1,604 service connections over a State-published service-area boundary.
principles.signal: SDWIS Community water system; SABL service-area boundary (verified); connections defined.

principles.name: Rules fit local conditions
principles.evidence_reason: The record documents how charges are set, whether a filed metered rate schedule or a share-and-acreage allocation, so cost tracks service. Whether every tier scales precisely with use is only partially visible at this scale, but a real cost-to-service rule is on record.
principles.finding: Charges are tied to service under a documented rate or share-based allocation rule reported to the State or set in the company's structure.
principles.signal: eAR Section 8a customer charges; documented rate or share-allocation rule.

principles.name: Collective-choice arrangements
principles.evidence_reason: The record documents a collective-choice mechanism: customers are shareholders who elect a named board that governs the company. Turnout and specific member votes on major decisions are not documented, but the elected-board structure and its membership are on record.
principles.finding: The company is owned by its customer-shareholders and run by a named board they elect, documented in its Form 990 governance section.
principles.signal: Mutual ownership; named elected board of directors (Form 990).

principles.name: Monitoring
principles.evidence_reason: Operational monitoring is documented: the State rates the system Not Failing on its drinking-water risk assessment and the system files an annual eAR. No independent audited financial statement is published, so financial monitoring is weaker, but the operational record is present.
principles.finding: The system is metered and monitored: the State SAFER risk assessment shows it Not Failing, and it files an annual eAR.
principles.signal: SAFER Not Failing; annual eAR reporting; metered connections.

principles.name: Graduated sanctions
principles.evidence_reason: No public record of a graduated shut-off or penalty policy was found for a system this small. NOT DOCUMENTED means the supporting record was not found, not that the company governs badly. It marks a gap in the documentary record, an evidence gap to close, never a governance failing.
principles.finding: No published shut-off, penalty, or delinquency policy was found for this system.
principles.signal: No sourced sanctions policy.

principles.name: Conflict-resolution mechanisms
principles.evidence_reason: No public record of a member dispute or conflict-resolution procedure was found. NOT DOCUMENTED means the supporting record was not found, not that the company governs badly. It marks a gap in the documentary record, an evidence gap to close, never a governance failing.
principles.finding: No published bylaws, dispute procedure, or grievance mechanism was found for this system.
principles.signal: No sourced conflict-resolution record.

principles.name: Recognized right to organize
principles.evidence_reason: Baseline legal standing is documented: the company is an incorporated mutual recognized by the IRS as a tax-exempt filer and by the State Water Board as a regulated water system. This records the right to organize as a member entity, not a documented instance of exercising it. The California Secretary of State holds the company as a registered corporation, entity number 0108768, first registered 04/07/1924, status as filed "Active", with a governing body named in the Statement of Information filed 6/23/2026. That is a direct state record of the right to organize being recognized, so the evidence behind this status is now a filed corporate record rather than an inference from the company's tax form. The status was already DOCUMENTED and does not move.
principles.finding: An incorporated California mutual water company recognized by the IRS (501(c)(12)) and by the State Water Board as a public water system.
principles.signal: IRS 501(c)(12) exempt filer (Form 990); SDWIS public water system.

principles.name: Nested enterprises
principles.evidence_reason: Nesting is documented on the supply side: SDWIS records the system as buying treated surface water wholesale, so it sits inside a larger regional supplier's system. Its role in basin or regional governance is not documented, so the nesting on record is physical rather than a governed layer.
principles.finding: The system buys treated water wholesale from a larger supplier, so it is nested inside a regional water enterprise.
principles.signal: SDWIS Primary Water Source Type: purchased surface water.

member_vs_customer.explainer: In a mutual water company a MEMBER is a shareholder who owns part of the system; a CUSTOMER is a metered service connection that receives water. pwss_volume.title: Water volume history (DWR PWSS survey)

calendar_basis.short: Calendar year, not the fiscal year ending June 30
calendar_basis.label: Different reporting periods. The DWR PWSS survey year is a calendar year ending December 31; this system's fiscal year ends June 30. A fiscal year therefore shares six of its twelve months with the calendar year it is named for and the other six with the calendar year before it. Read the two side by side with that in mind. Neither series is recast: both are reported as filed. The survey year runs January to December, with the filed annual total reported as filed and never computed from the twelve months.

eras.label: DWR PWSS, 2006-2022 form (adds untreated water from 2007)
State Water Board SAFER, 2023-2024 form (splits self-produced from obtained, and potable from non-potable)

rollup.title: Derived comparability view (customer type by water quality)
rollup.note: DERIVED, medium confidence, and shown beside the as-filed classes above, never in place of them. Every figure here is a sum of the filed class figures named on each cell; nothing is estimated and no filed value is altered. Two axes rather than four buckets because the filed classes are not mutually exclusive: the 2023-2024 form files residential non-potable deliveries, which belong to both. Commercial and institutional share one filed column and are not separable from the source, so the bucket keeps both words. The filed urban total is the potable total, so potable buckets reconcile against it and any difference is shown as a residual rather than absorbed; non-potable sits outside it by the survey's own design. A year in which a filed unit could not be recognized is marked incomplete, because the convertible subset is not the system's total. The filed urban total covers URBAN potable deliveries only: agricultural irrigation sits outside it, as does every non-potable class, by the survey's own design and not because anything is missing. Both are reported separately beside it.

coverage.filed: 12 survey years, 2013 to 2024. Production carries a positive figure in all 12 of those years, across 3 sources. Deliveries carry a positive figure in only 5 of the 12 years, across 5 customer classes.
coverage.tail: Separately, 89 cells were filed as zero, which is a figure the system reported and not an absence, and 7 were left blank. 15 figures carry a unit the survey's code list does not contain; those are shown as filed and were not converted, because a guessed unit would be a guessed volume.
coverage.assurance: This data was pulled and verified in full. The thinness above is what Pleasant Valley Mutual Water Company filed with the survey, not a gap in what we retrieved. Its production filing is complete over the same period, which is the clearest evidence that the pull worked.

pwss_volume.note: Annual water volume as filed with the California Department of Water Resources Public Water System Statistics survey, 2013 to 2024. Each system chooses its own unit of measure and the choice is not stable from year to year, so the acre-feet column is a DERIVED normalization at medium confidence and the filed value and its unit, shown on hover and in the logic panel, are the source of truth at high confidence. Years this system did not file are absent rather than zero. For 2013 and later the State Water Board (eAR and SAFER) is the standard and this DWR series is a backup, except the 2023-2024 SAFER years, which are Water Boards data. Nothing here is reconciled against another source.

sgma_basin.title: Groundwater basin (DWR, SGMA)

basins.name: PLEASANT VALLEY
basins.plain_lead: The Department of Water Resources ranks this basin High priority, its top tier, and has designated it in critical overdraft: the state has found the basin is being pumped faster than it naturally refills. That is a supply-risk signal about the basin itself, not a finding about this system. A Groundwater Sustainability Agency is the local body SGMA makes responsible for bringing a basin into balance. 3 agencies are named for this basin, listed below.
basins.gsa_text: Camrosa Water District GSA - Pleasant Valley; County of Ventura GSA - Pleasant Valley Basin Outlying Areas; Fox Canyon Groundwater Management Agency GSA - Pleasant Valley
basins.gw_level_comment:
CRITICAL OVERDRAFT 2016
Source: 4-006_7a_Hydrographs_PleasantValley.pdf

2) The 2016 Annual GW Conditions Report states that there is long-term overdraft for several decades in the Pleastant Valley groundwater basin.
Source:  4-006_7a_2016GWConditionsReportFINAL.pdf  pg. 12
basins.subsidence_comment:
1) "Steady increase in water use has resulted in seawater intrusion, inter-aquifer flow, land subsidence, and ground-water contamination."
Source: USGS WRI Report 2002-4136:  Source: 4-006_7b_SimulationofgroundwaterSurfaceWaterFlowinSantaClara-CalleguarsBasinVenturaCountyCa.pdf

Misc. - Indirect evidence of subsidence related to groundwater withdrawal, groundwater level declines greater than 30m, subsurface collapse of well casings, and repeated re-leveling of irrigated fields

basins.subsidence_comment:
1) According to the report (wri024136), Water-level declines in the basin have induced land subsidence that was first measured in 1939 and have resulted in as much as 2.7 feet land subsidence in the southern part of the Oxnard Plain. The model simulated a total of 3 feet of land subsidence in the southern part of the Oxnard Plain and as much as 5 feet in the Las Posas Valley subbasins. Model simulations indicate that most of the land subsidence occurred after the drought of the late 1920s and during the agricultural expansion of the 1950s and 1960s. The results also indicate that subsidence occurred primarily in the upper-aquifer system prior to 1959, but in the lower-aquifer system between 1959-93 owing to an increase in pumpage from the lower-aquifer system.
Source: 4-008_7b_SimulationofgroundwaterSurfaceWaterFlowinSantaClara-CalleguarsBasinVenturaCountyCa.pdf

2) Two continuous GPS site in the basin (VNCO in Ventura and P729 near El Rio) showing recent subsidence
Source: 4-008_7b_GPSStationP729 and 4-008_7b_GPSStationVNCO
basins.join_note: SABL boundary verification: Verified. The areal join is derived and never better than the boundary it rests on.

sgma_basin.plain_overdraft: What critical overdraft means: it is a designation the Department of Water Resources publishes for a basin it has found is being pumped faster than it naturally refills. It describes the basin, not any one system drawing from it, and it is carried here exactly as the state publishes it.
sgma_basin.note: Basin priority, critical overdraft designation and the governing agency are published by the Department of Water Resources and are carried exactly as published (high confidence). Placing this system in a basin is an AREAL join: its service-area boundary is overlapped with the basin boundary, so the placement is derived and is never better than the boundary it rests on. That is why the join confidence reads medium or low and never high. Where a service area spans more than one basin every basin is listed and none is ranked, because the source does not say how much of the area lies in each. The groundwater-level line is DWR's own written finding for the basin, quoted rather than scored; no well record is read.

sdwis_compliance.title: Drinking-water compliance (US EPA SDWIS)
sdwis_compliance.note: Violations and enforcement as recorded by the US EPA Envirofacts federal SDWIS mirror, carried exactly as published (high confidence). A violation is treated as open when the record carries no return-to-compliance date; that date is the evidence, and it remains the only thing the open reading rests on. Codes are shown as filed, with EPA's own name for each beside it; a code EPA's reference does not list is shown as the bare code and marked as unmatched.
sdwis_compliance.code_note: The detail column carries what the record says went wrong, exactly as filed, with EPA's own plain-language name beside each code. The names come from EPA's published SDWA reference code values, retrieved 2026-08-21, matched on the code exactly and never on a near match, so a name is a lookup rather than a reading (high confidence). A code the reference does not list keeps its raw code and is marked not matched; it is never guessed at, because a wrong name is worse than a bare number. Where the record carries a measured result it is shown in the unit it was filed in, beside the state limit it is measured against.

gap_evidence.why_note: Why federal mirror tables commonly disagree: Envirofacts is a mirror of the state's primacy record, and its tables are refreshed on their own schedules, so one table can carry a more recent load than another and the two read differently in between. A violation that was corrected, withdrawn or superseded in the primary table is also not always removed from the cross-reference rows that point at it. Which of those explains this system is not something the source states, so it is not claimed here.

safer_standing.plain_sentence: The State Water Board's SAFER assessment lists this system as Potentially At-Risk. Retrieved from the state's published file on 2026-08-27.

comparable.comparison_note: Two readings of the same indicator from two different bases. how_built.title: How this was built
how_built.intro: A plain account of the forensic lineage behind the hard-to-source metrics: what sources were checked, what was found, what was derived, and what could not be built and why. Every figure marked DERIVED or IMPOSSIBLE above is traceable to a line here.

sources_checked: State Water Board eAR Section 8b (water-rate revenue B1.1/B1.2)
State Water Board eAR Section 4 (connection count, same reporting year)
audited financial statement (secondary cross-check, where published)
entries.found: The eAR Section 8b reports water-rate revenue for reporting year 2023, so this is a DIRECT filed figure; per customer it is divided by the eAR Section 4 connection count for the same reporting year, so numerator and denominator share the year.

sources_checked: State Water Board eAR Section 8b (water-rate revenue B1.1/B1.2)
entries.found: A period-aligned residual cannot be computed for this filer, so the metric is rendered IMPOSSIBLE rather than guessed.
entries.note: Not derivable. The eAR Section 8b is the fiscal year ending July 19, 2023 while the Form 990 fiscal year ends June 30, 2023; the two period ends are 1 months apart, so a period-aligned residual cannot be computed.

sources_checked: State Water Board eAR Section 8a (rate prices)
State Water Board eAR Section 8b (revenue lines)
entries.found: The rate price exists in Section 8a but no revenue or tier volume is reported, and the base charge is already inside water sales.
entries.note: The eAR Section 8a reports a base/meter rate PRICE, but the filing carries no meter revenue line and no tier volume, and the base charge is already inside the water-sales revenue (eAR Section 8b water rates). Building a separate meter figure would double-count. Not backed into from a total.

No filing states a member/shareholder count, so the per-member unit economics read not reported rather than borrowing the connection count.
Volume delivered in acre-feet is not in the Form 990 and the CCR states only a source mix, so the per-acre-foot metrics read not reported; the eAR Section 6 is named as the source still needed.

blocks.title: Who they are
blocks.body: A California mutual water company (501(c)(12)) serving about 1,600 service connections and roughly 5,000 residents in Camarillo, Ventura County, on the flat Pleasant Valley floor. [C][E][1] Owned by its customer-shareholders and run not for profit. [990]

blocks.title: How the money works
blocks.body: Revenue of about $2,745,256 in FY2025, from water charges and assessments to member-shareholders. [D] The State Water Board eAR Section 8b for reporting year 2023 reported total revenue of $2,176,820 and total expenses of $2,176,820, on the filer's own self-reported basis. [E] A detailed rate history beyond the filed schedule is not reported.

blocks.title: Where the water comes from
blocks.body: Supply blends local Ventura County groundwater (the Pleasant Valley basin) with wholesale imported water from Calleguas Municipal Water District, which delivers State Water Project water via Metropolitan Water District. [1][2] SDWIS classifies the primary source as purchased surface water. [C]

blocks.title: Infrastructure and its age
blocks.body: Plant is read from the Form 990 balance sheet; the computed net plant age (accumulated depreciation as a share of gross plant) is shown with its multi-year trend. [990][D] Detailed infrastructure history is not reported in a public source.

source_lines: Form 990 Part X line 10a (land, buildings, and equipment; gross)
Form 990 Part X line 10b (accumulated depreciation)
net_plant_age.logic: Accumulated depreciation as a share of gross plant (Form 990 Part X line 10b over line 10a): the portion of the system's plant already depreciated, a proxy for average plant age. A falling trend means reinvestment is renewing the plant faster than it wears down. This shares its inputs with the Asset Consumption Ratio on the tearsheet.
net_plant_age.confidence_reason: A ratio derived from two filed Part X figures; medium per the BLUEPRINT confidence tiers (a derivation, not a direct line item).
net_plant_age.what_would_change: nothing; the value is comparable as filed

blocks.title: How they got here
blocks.body: The company traces to the early twentieth century (IRS mutual recognition dates to 1937) and serves the agricultural-turned-suburban Pleasant Valley around Camarillo; a detailed founding narrative is not published. [990][1]

blocks.title: Who runs it and how
blocks.body: Governed by a shareholder-elected board (President James Graham and four directors in FY2025) with a Water Superintendent and operators; the board meets monthly and meetings are open to the public. [1][990] The company publishes water-quality reports and program materials on its website. [1]

blocks.title: On the record
blocks.body: State drinking-water compliance standing is shown below from the SAFER risk assessment. [S] The company issued and later lifted a water alert, with follow-up testing reported as confirming the water safe, and implemented a new rate structure in 2024; exact dates are not stated. [1]

compliance.source: California State Water Resources Control Board, Division of Drinking Water: SAFER Drinking Water Risk Assessment Public Flat File, data.ca.gov resource 255887bb-5451-4c19-8e35-27899ae8c3ad

blocks.title: Strengths
blocks.body: The larger of the small Camarillo mutuals, with a blended groundwater-plus-imported supply that reduces single-source risk. [1][2] Active, transparent governance: monthly open board meetings and published reports. [1] Metered connections with a filed, recently updated rate structure. [1][E]

blocks.title: Weak points and watch items
blocks.body: Imported water exposes it to Calleguas and State Water Project rate increases and drought allocation cuts. [1][2] A past water alert, since resolved, shows the quality-monitoring burden a small system carries. [1] At roughly 1,600 connections it is still small, so fixed costs land on a limited base.

weather_exposure.title: Weather exposure
weather_exposure.lead: A computed read, not a self-report. Three separately sourced components: how much of the service area sits in mapped fire hazard, how much of this company's own filing window its county spent in severe drought, and how exposed its water supply is to a dry year. Each carries its own source and check date, and a component that cannot be computed says so rather than going blank.

composite.basis: Composed from 3 of 3 components (Fire hazard, Drought regime, Supply sensitivity).

components.name: Fire hazard
components.value: About 64.1% of the service area sits in the High or Very High fire hazard zones California maps, and the most severe class mapped there is Very High.

detail.label: Highest class touching the service area
Share in High or Very High
Very High zone
detail.value: about 64.1% of the service area (637.0 acres), LRA, SRA

components.confidence_reason: SABL boundary verification: Verified. The areal join is derived and never better than the boundary it rests on, so it is never high. The share is integrated over 600 scan rows of about 3.66 m, so it is approximate to that resolution and is not an exact acreage.
components.source: CAL FIRE Fire Hazard Severity Zones (fhsz24_1), State and Local Responsibility Areas, intersected with the State Water Board SABL service-area boundary
components.logic: The service-area boundary the State Water Board publishes is laid over the fire hazard severity zones CAL FIRE publishes, and the share of the service area inside each class is measured. High and Very High are reported together because those are the classes California attaches building and defensible-space requirements to.
